Title: Working space about electrical equipment
Our paraphrase: Leave at least 1 m of clear working space about electrical equipment wherever it must be reached for operation or maintenance. This covers the front and, where access is needed there, the sides or back. Add any extra room that draw-out devices such as breakers or starters need when fully withdrawn.

Title: Location of the consumer's service equipment
Our paraphrase: Put the consumer's service equipment where it is readily accessible and close to where the service conductors enter the building. It does not belong in places such as clothes closets, bathrooms, stairways or spaces with low headroom.

Title: Grounding electrodes
Our paraphrase: The code names what can serve as a grounding electrode for a system. A manufactured electrode is normally two rods, each 3 m long, driven in full length, spaced at least 3 m apart and bonded together. Whether a buried metal water pipe may serve as an electrode depends on the province.

Title: Interconnection of grounding electrodes
Our paraphrase: Connect together all the grounding electrodes at a building, such as ground rods and a water pipe electrode, so that they act as one grounding system.

Title: Equipotential bonding of non-electrical equipment
Our paraphrase: Metal piping and other non-electrical equipment that could become energized are bonded to the electrical grounding system. This includes the building's metal water piping, which is bonded with a bonding conductor.

Title: Rating of overcurrent devices
Our paraphrase: An overcurrent device generally cannot be rated above the ampacity of the conductors it protects. For copper conductors from 14 AWG to 10 AWG the maximum device rating is 15 A for 14 AWG, 20 A for 12 AWG and 30 A for 10 AWG. A few small cords and wires, and the Table 13 correlation, have their own exceptions.

Title: Mounting height of branch-circuit overcurrent devices in dwellings
Our paraphrase: In a dwelling unit, mount no branch-circuit breaker or switch with its handle more than 1.7 m above the finished floor. The main is excepted.

Title: Arc-fault protection in dwelling units
Our paraphrase: Branch circuits that supply 125 V receptacles rated 20 A or less in a dwelling need combination-type AFCI protection. Listed locations are exempt, such as refrigerator receptacles, kitchen counter, island and peninsula receptacles, and bathroom receptacles within 1 m of the wash basin.

Concern: Draft from public summaries: check rule number, sub-item and edition
Title: Receptacles near sinks and wet areas
Our paraphrase: A 5-15R or 5-20R receptacle within 1.5 m of a sink, bathtub or shower stall, or outdoors within 2.5 m of finished grade, needs Class A GFCI protection. The exception is a receptacle behind a fixed appliance, such as a clothes washer, that portable appliances cannot reach. A Class A GFCI opens the circuit at a ground-fault current of 6 mA or more, and never below 4 mA.

Title: Receptacles in dwelling units
Our paraphrase: Place dwelling-unit receptacles in finished walls so that every spot along the floor line of usable wall space (an unbroken run of 900 mm or more) is within 1.8 m of one. The practical maximum gap between two receptacles is therefore 3.6 m.

Concern: Draft from public summaries: check rule number, sub-item and edition
Title: Receptacles at kitchen counter work surfaces
Our paraphrase: Behind kitchen counter work surfaces, install split receptacles so that you are never farther than 900 mm, measured along the wall line, from one. Sinks, built-in equipment and isolated work surfaces shorter than 300 mm at the wall line do not count.

Concern: Draft from public summaries: check rule number, sub-item and edition
Title: Location of motor disconnecting means
Our paraphrase: Install a motor's disconnecting means in sight of the motor and its starter, and within 9 m of them.
